title: AI scams in Georgia and South Florida: How scammers use deepfakes to steal millions

reading.body:
Criminals are using generative AI to create deepfakes and voice clones for fraud, impersonating real people to target victims. A South Florida immigration attorney discovered his voice had been cloned to solicit money from immigrants. This is an impersonation attack enabled by AI, where the technology generates realistic but false representations of identifiable individuals to establish false trust.

The scam operated on social media and through phone calls, where victims encountered what appeared to be legitimate professionals or family members. The criminals combined voice cloning with research about victims' circumstances to make their schemes more persuasive. Detection would have required victims to verify identities through independent channels before sending money, such as calling known phone numbers or using pre-arranged code words.

Whether these systems were deliberately designed by their creators to enable fraud is not established. The reports document that criminals obtained and repurposed the technology for impersonation, but do not establish the intent or knowledge of the developers who built the underlying AI tools.

summary:
Scammers are increasingly using artificial intelligence technology to create convincing deepfakes and voice clones for fraud schemes across Georgia and South Florida. A South Florida immigration attorney discovered criminals had cloned his voice to target immigrants, while a Cobb County couple lost approximately $800,000 in a cryptocurrency scam. According to the FBI's 2025 Internet Crime Report, Americans reported nearly $893 million in AI-enabled scam losses last year. Florida reported 350 AI-related complaints with $39.9 million in losses, while Georgia had 71 complaints totaling $10.4 million in losses.

Criminals are using generative AI to make traditional scams more believable by cloning voices from social media, spoofing phone numbers, creating fake photographs, and researching victims' family connections. The technology is being used in romance scams, investment schemes, emergency phone calls, and grandparent scams where AI mimics a relative's voice. Federal investigators note these figures likely undercount the actual problem since many victims don't report scams. Authorities recommend families establish code words to verify identity, verify urgent requests through trusted phone numbers, and pause before sending money in response to unexpected communications.
